answer.rationale: The tempting move is switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor, because memory_c2 says exactly that worked and the quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate. But c2 is the memory whose original context matters most: 'onboarding was quick' may have been recorded under slack capacity, not at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer and 14 days to contract expiry. A migration that slips even one delivery cycle breaks the no-added-delivery-risk constraint, and cost savings do not recover a stopped line. So I verify c2 (does the source record show onboarding conditions comparable to today, and on this component at this volume?) and c4 (does the source record show benchmarking actually moved price by a magnitude near 18%, or only a few points plus payment terms?). With one decision available, negotiate_terms is the choice that can capture the mandate without touching the physical supply path: the low-cost quote is live leverage, c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on price and terms, and c6 says a longer commitment unlocks volume pricing without narrowing scope, so an 18% target is plausibly reachable by combining term length with the benchmark. c1 supports that holding the incumbent integration costs nothing operationally. Downstream risk I am flagging rather than resolving: negotiating an 18% cut may quietly buy back the savings as reduced priority, thinner allocation, or slower expedites during a shortage, and the single-point-of-failure that c3 was about remains unaddressed — add_second_source is the right next-cycle move once buffer exists. If verification shows c4's recovery was only marginal and c2's onboarding truly was low-risk and comparable, I would shift toward a staged qualification of the low-cost vendor as a second source rather than an outright primary switch, and would not switch primary supply while the line has no buffer.
